item.title: Fixing JavaScript Module Scope Issues: Accessing Exported Functions Globally
item.description:
“Fixing JavaScript Module Scope Issues: Accessing Exported Functions Globally”

When employing JavaScript ES6 modules (<script type="module">), functions or variables defined within that module are typically confined to the module scope. Attempting to call these exports directly from global scope (e.g., an inline onclick attribute in HTML) results in a ReferenceError. How can we reliably bridge this module scope barrier to invoke these exported functions when needed globally or from unrelated parts of the application?

item.title: JavaScript Module Export Best Practices: Static Methods vs. Named Exports
item.description:
“JavaScript Module Export Best Practices: Static Methods vs. Named Exports”

When developing utility functions in JavaScript, a common initial approach involves grouping them within a class using only static methods. Experts frequently flag this structure as a potential “code smell.” Why should developers favor simpler module exports over this class-based pattern for static utilities?

The Module Pattern as a Superior Alternative to Static Classes

If the goal is simply to expose a collection of related functions, instantiating a class solely for its static members introduces unnecessary boilerplate. A more idiomatic ECMAScript 6 (ES6) approach is to export a plain object containing these methods directly from the module.

item.title: JavaScript ES6 Imports: Curly Braces Explained
item.description:
“JavaScript ES6 Imports: Curly Braces Explained”

When working with modern JavaScript, particularly ES6 modules, understanding how to import functionality from other files is crucial. A common point of inquiry revolves around the use of curly braces {} within import statements. This post delves into the distinct roles of default and named exports and clarifies precisely when and why curly braces are employed.

The Core Distinction: Default vs. Named Exports

At its heart, the use of curly braces in JavaScript imports hinges on how modules export their contents.
